areas.title: Mathematics
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Proof is thinking made visible. A model can algebra-crunch; it cannot replace the habit of inventing a definition, seeing a structure, or knowing when an argument is wrong.

areas.title: Statistics
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: The scarce skill is asking the right question under uncertainty, not plugging numbers into a library.

areas.title: Computer science foundations
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Mental models of what computation is — abstraction, systems, algorithms as ideas — outlast any particular API. Trivia that a model can spit out is deprioritized.

areas.title: AI / ML / LLMs
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: The point is to understand these systems well enough to steer and evaluate them, not to collect framework tutorials a model already writes.

areas.title: AI safety and alignment
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Judgment about what we should build, and how to tell that a safety claim is real, will not be automated away.

areas.title: AI security
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Adversarial thinking about systems that change quickly. Prefer recent university material and living checklists over stale slide decks.

areas.title: Physics
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: First-principles models of the world. Deriving a conservation law by hand is a kind of intelligence no autocomplete substitutes for.

areas.title: Chemistry
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: A feel for matter, equilibrium, and mechanism — the physical vocabulary underneath biology and materials.

areas.title: Biology
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: What a living system actually is. Summaries are cheap; the ability to reason about information flow in a cell is not.

areas.title: Engineering
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Making something work in the world, with models you can defend when the artifact misbehaves.

areas.title: Economics
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Models of choice, constraint, and interaction. Useful as thinking tools, not as forecast trivia.

areas.title: History
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Judgment from particular cases. A model can summarize a century; it cannot remember it for you or decide what the analogy is allowed to prove.

areas.title: Philosophy
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Examining premises and making arguments precise. That is the opposite of accepting a fluent paragraph.

areas.title: Literature (Western)
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Attention, moral imagination, and a language larger than the present. Great books train taste that autocomplete cannot borrow.

areas.title: Literature (Chinese)
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Another civilization's thought, in its own sentences. Reading 論語 or 紅樓夢 slowly is not a task to delegate.

areas.title: Mandarin (Traditional, advanced)
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Advanced literacy in Traditional Chinese, especially 文言, is a long human skill. It is a way into texts, not a streak.

areas.title: Theology and Bible
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Ultimate questions and close reading of scripture. The work is formation and argument, not trivia.

areas.title: Writing and rhetoric
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Writing is how thought becomes checkable. An essay you wrestle onto the page is not the same as a generated draft.

areas.title: Music and art
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Perception and taste. Learning to hear form in a Bach movement is not a summarization task.

areas.title: Creativity and invention
areas.why_this_outlasts_ai: Posing problems, inventing, noticing, and building. That is upstream of any tool: heuristics (Polya), taste (Hamming), design, puzzles, and making things.

items.title: MIT 18.01SC Single Variable Calculus
items.why_canonical: Standard first-year calculus at MIT, with recitation problems and exams. Rigetti treats a full calculus sequence as the start of an undergraduate math education. Karpathy named calculus (with linear algebra) as a baseline.
items.one_liner: Standard first-year calculus at MIT, with recitation problems and exams.

items.title: MIT 18.02SC Multivariable Calculus
items.why_canonical: The natural second semester after 18.01 in MIT sequence; needed for electricity and magnetism and for machine learning gradients.
items.one_liner: The natural second semester after 18.01 in MIT sequence; needed for electricity and magnetism and for machine learning gradients.

items.title: MIT 18.06 Linear Algebra
items.why_canonical: Rigetti calls Strang essential and especially good for independent study. Teach Yourself CS also points to Strang for linear algebra.
items.one_liner: Rigetti calls Strang essential and especially good for independent study.

items.title: How to Prove It
items.why_canonical: Rigetti essential introduction-to-proofs text. She also supplements with Polya How to Solve It, which Teach Yourself CS independently recommends.
items.one_liner: Rigetti essential introduction-to-proofs text.

items.title: Understanding Analysis
items.why_canonical: Rigetti essential real-analysis pairing: Abbott plus Rudin Principles of Mathematical Analysis.
items.one_liner: Rigetti essential real-analysis pairing: Abbott plus Rudin Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

items.title: Harvard Stat 110: Probability
items.why_canonical: Harvard flagship undergraduate probability course, with lecture videos and a large practice bank. The usual gateway before CS229-style machine learning.
items.one_liner: Harvard flagship undergraduate probability course, with lecture videos and a large practice bank.

items.title: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs + Berkeley CS 61A (Harvey)
items.instructor: Abelson, Sussman, and Sussman; videos by Brian Harvey
items.why_canonical: Teach Yourself CS programming pick. They say SICP can change how you think about programs, and they recommend at least the first three chapters and the exercises — already a core-versus-optional split.
items.one_liner: Teach Yourself CS programming pick.

items.title: CMU 15-213 / Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective
items.why_canonical: Teach Yourself CS's favorite intro systems book, and one of the two books they would keep if they could only keep two. They say a typical course covers most of chapters 1-6. OSSU lists Nand2Tetris in core systems and points at intro-computer-systems labs (CSAPP-style) in extras.
items.one_liner: Teach Yourself CS's favorite intro systems book, and one of the two books they would keep if they could only keep two.

items.title: MIT 6.006 Introduction to Algorithms
items.why_canonical: MIT standard algorithms course with open problem sets. TYCS prefers Skiena Algorithm Design Manual as a book; 6.006 is the free course that can be written by hand.
items.one_liner: MIT standard algorithms course with open problem sets.

items.title: MIT 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science
items.instructor: Tom Leighton and Marten van Dijk
items.why_canonical: TYCS pick for Math for CS: logic, combinatorics, discrete probability, graphs, some number theory.
items.one_liner: TYCS pick for Math for CS: logic, combinatorics, discrete probability, graphs, some number theory.

items.title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces
items.why_canonical: TYCS OS book, preferred over the dinosaur book for clarity and self-study.
items.one_liner: TYCS OS book, preferred over the dinosaur book for clarity and self-study.

items.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
items.why_canonical: TYCS distributed-systems pick and the other book in their if-only-two-books pair with CSAPP.
items.one_liner: TYCS distributed-systems pick and the other book in their if-only-two-books pair with CSAPP.

items.title: Stanford CS229 Machine Learning
items.instructor: Historically Andrew Ng; current staff on the course site
items.why_canonical: Stanford standard ML course. TYCS names Ng and this style of course as the ML starting point. CS336 lists CS229 or equivalent among prerequisites.
items.one_liner: Stanford standard ML course.

items.title: Stanford CS224N NLP with Deep Learning
items.why_canonical: Stanford standard deep-learning NLP course; usual next step toward transformers after CS229. CS336 lists it among ML prerequisites.
items.one_liner: Stanford standard deep-learning NLP course; usual next step toward transformers after CS229.

items.title: Stanford CS336 Language Modeling from Scratch
items.why_canonical: Current Stanford course that walks through building a language model end-to-end: data, tokenizer, transformer, training, scaling, alignment/RL. Directly relevant to lab work.
items.one_liner: Current Stanford course that walks through building a language model end-to-end: data, tokenizer, transformer, training, scaling, alignment/RL.

items.title: Stanford CS231n Deep Learning for Computer Vision
items.instructor: Originally Fei-Fei Li, Andrej Karpathy, Justin Johnson
items.why_canonical: Karpathy taught it and later told someone to take EECS 498 and/or CS231n and complete all of the programming assignments. That advice is stricter than the completion rule; both facts stay visible.
items.one_liner: Karpathy taught it and later told someone to take EECS 498 and/or CS231n and complete all of the programming assignments.

items.title: Neural Networks: Zero to Hero
items.why_canonical: Karpathy own series, announced on X; he later said beginners should watch the playlist from the start, in order.
items.one_liner: Karpathy own series, announced on X; he later said beginners should watch the playlist from the start, in order.

items.title: BlueDot Impact: AI Alignment
items.instructor: BlueDot Impact; 2022 curriculum originally designed by Richard Ngo
items.why_canonical: Living version of the field standard intro sequence. Ngo designed the 2022 AGI Safety Fundamentals alignment curriculum that BlueDot ran, and pointed at oversight, interpretability, and this curriculum.
items.one_liner: Living version of the field standard intro sequence.

items.title: Intro to ML Safety
items.instructor: Dan Hendrycks / Center for AI Safety
items.institution: Dan Hendrycks / Center for AI Safety
items.why_canonical: A full technical safety course covering robustness, monitoring, control, systemic safety, and x-risk arguments. Requires prior ML/deep learning.
items.one_liner: A full technical safety course covering robustness, monitoring, control, systemic safety, and x-risk arguments.

items.title: Mechanistic interpretability (Nanda, Olah, ARENA)
items.instructor: Neel Nanda; Chris Olah / Anthropic Circuits

items.one_liner: Olah pointed people at Nanda annotated reading list.

items.title: Adversarial robustness and trojans (from Intro to ML Safety)
items.why_canonical: Free technical treatment of attacks (PGD, transferability, text attacks) and hidden functionality (trojans/poisoning). Open university AI-security courses with problem sets are otherwise thin.
items.one_liner: Free technical treatment of attacks (PGD, transferability, text attacks) and hidden functionality (trojans/poisoning).

items.title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications
items.why_canonical: Industry-standard enumeration of LLM application failures (prompt injection, insecure output handling, data poisoning, supply chain, etc.). Not a university course and not attributed to a researcher tweet; included because it is the document security teams point at.
items.one_liner: Industry-standard enumeration of LLM application failures (prompt injection, insecure output handling, data poisoning, supply chain, etc.).

items.title: Stanford XACS134 AI Security
items.why_canonical: Named Stanford course on prompt injection, poisoning, extraction, RAG/agent risks, and defenses.
items.one_liner: Named Stanford course on prompt injection, poisoning, extraction, RAG/agent risks, and defenses.

items.one_liner: MIT first physics course.

items.one_liner: Second semester of MIT physics; Rigetti electrostatics/electrodynamics arc.

items.one_liner: Rigetti: essential reading, on every amateur and professional physicist shelf, and the book that pulled her into physics.

items.why_canonical: The standard modern introduction to Christian belief in the Anglican/evangelical world requested here. Not found as a St. John assignment; included because Lewis was named, not because a tweet did.
items.one_liner: The standard modern introduction to Christian belief in the Anglican/evangelical world requested here.

items.title: The Reason for God
items.why_canonical: The widely used contemporary apologetics companion to Lewis, included because Keller was named.
items.one_liner: The widely used contemporary apologetics companion to Lewis, included because Keller was named.

items.title: How to Read a Book
items.instructor: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
items.institution: Mortimer Adler and Charles Van Doren
items.why_canonical: The standard modern guide to inspectional, analytical, and syntopical reading — the skill this shelf is for.
items.one_liner: The standard modern guide to inspectional, analytical, and syntopical reading — the skill this shelf is for.

items.title: The Age of the Essay; Write Simply; How to Write Usefully
items.why_canonical: Graham own essays on what an essay is, how to write plainly, and how to write something true. Direct primary sources.
items.one_liner: Graham own essays on what an essay is, how to write plainly, and how to write something true.

items.title: Yale MUSI 112: Listening to Music
items.why_canonical: The standard open course in hearing how Western music is put together: rhythm, melody, harmony, form; Bach and Mozart through later styles.
items.one_liner: The standard open course in hearing how Western music is put together: rhythm, melody, harmony, form; Bach and Mozart through later styles.

items.title: Nand2Tetris (The Elements of Computing Systems)
items.why_canonical: Teach Yourself CS names Nand2Tetris as the gentler, cohesive intro to how a computer is built, recommending the first six chapters and projects. OSSU places From Nand to Tetris in core systems and links this site as the alternative to a platform course.
items.one_liner: Teach Yourself CS names Nand2Tetris as the gentler, cohesive intro to how a computer is built, recommending the first six chapters and projects.

items.title: MIT 6.046J Design and Analysis of Algorithms
items.instructor: Erik Demaine, Srini Devadas, and Nancy Lynch
items.why_canonical: MIT's intermediate algorithms course: divide-and-conquer, randomization, DP, greedy methods, complexity. Teach Yourself CS emphasizes algorithms as essential; 6.046 is the deeper MIT course after 6.006.
items.one_liner: MIT's intermediate algorithms course: divide-and-conquer, randomization, DP, greedy methods, complexity.

items.title: MIT 6.1810 Operating System Engineering
items.why_canonical: MIT's undergraduate OS engineering course: you extend a small Unix-like kernel. OSSU extras list Operating System Engineering. Teach Yourself CS recommends xv6-style work after OSTEP.
items.one_liner: MIT's undergraduate OS engineering course: you extend a small Unix-like kernel.

items.title: Stanford CS144 / Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking
items.instructor: Stanford CS144 staff; Kurose and Ross (book)
items.why_canonical: Teach Yourself CS names Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach as their favorite networking book and Stanford CS144 as the lecture series. OSSU core systems assigns the same book with the authors' lectures and Wireshark labs.
items.one_liner: Teach Yourself CS names Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach as their favorite networking book and Stanford CS144 as the lecture series.

items.title: CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems
items.why_canonical: CMU's well-known systems course in which you build pieces of a database. Public notes and projects (BusTub) are posted on the course site.
items.one_liner: CMU's well-known systems course in which you build pieces of a database.

items.title: Crafting Interpreters
items.why_canonical: Teach Yourself CS's suggested introductory compilers text: free online, written for self-study, with challenges throughout.
items.one_liner: Teach Yourself CS's suggested introductory compilers text: free online, written for self-study, with challenges throughout.

items.title: Stanford CS143 Compilers
items.why_canonical: Stanford's undergraduate compilers course on its own site, with the usual lexer-parser-semantic-codegen arc.
items.one_liner: Stanford's undergraduate compilers course on its own site, with the usual lexer-parser-semantic-codegen arc.

items.title: MIT 6.5840 Distributed Systems
items.why_canonical: Teach Yourself CS recommends MIT 6.824 as the video/graduate course in distributed systems, alongside Kleppmann's book. 6.5840 is the current number for that course. OSSU extras point at 6.824.
items.one_liner: Teach Yourself CS recommends MIT 6.824 as the video/graduate course in distributed systems, alongside Kleppmann's book.

items.title: CMU 10-414/714 Deep Learning Systems
items.why_canonical: A university systems course on how deep learning frameworks actually work: automatic differentiation, efficient kernels, parallelism. Complements CS336's language-modeling-from-scratch path.
items.one_liner: A university systems course on how deep learning frameworks actually work: automatic differentiation, efficient kernels, parallelism.

items.title: MIT 6.858 Computer Systems Security
items.instructor: MIT CSAIL (Nickolai Zeldovich and staff in recent offerings)
items.why_canonical: MIT's course on designing and attacking secure systems: OS security, isolation, web security, labs that build and break a system. Requested as the security backbone of the CS track.
items.one_liner: MIT's course on designing and attacking secure systems: OS security, isolation, web security, labs that build and break a system.

items.title: How to Solve It
items.why_canonical: The classic book on heuristic problem solving. Teach Yourself CS recommends it as a unique guide to general problem solving, as applicable to CS as to mathematics. Rigetti also names it as a supplement to How to Prove It.
items.one_liner: The classic book on heuristic problem solving.

items.title: The Art of Doing Science and Engineering
items.why_canonical: Hamming's lectures on how to do important work, how to think, and how to style a life around problems. Teach Yourself CS quotes Hamming ('think before you write'); this book is the full treatment of that ethos.
items.one_liner: Hamming's lectures on how to do important work, how to think, and how to style a life around problems.

items.title: Stanford d.school open design tools
items.why_canonical: Stanford d.school's own published methods for need-finding, framing, prototyping, and testing. Included as the open design-thinking materials, not because a third party ranked a MOOC.
items.one_liner: Stanford d.school's own published methods for need-finding, framing, prototyping, and testing.

items.title: MIT 2.009 Product Engineering Process
items.why_canonical: MIT's famous invention and product-engineering course: go from a vague need to a working artifact. The process, not the final contest, is the point.
items.one_liner: MIT's famous invention and product-engineering course: go from a vague need to a working artifact.

items.title: Art of Problem Solving style puzzles
items.why_canonical: The named style of hard, inventive math puzzles requested for the creativity thread. It trains posing and turning a problem, which is what calculation software does not do for you.
items.one_liner: The named style of hard, inventive math puzzles requested for the creativity thread.

items.title: Stanford CS234 Reinforcement Learning
items.why_canonical: A current introduction to reinforcement learning, with public lecture slides and written and coding assignments that include deep RL and a first look at RLHF.
items.one_liner: A current introduction to reinforcement learning, with public lecture slides and written and coding assignments that include deep RL and a first look at RLHF.
